source.title: Towards Combinatorial Interpretability of Neural Computation
source.authors: Micah Adler; Dan Alistarh; N. Shavit

page_placements.theme: Toy models: where superposition and polysemanticity come from, and their geometry

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present
record.tranche_reason: The paper's own small-network results show polysemantic neurons and argues that overlapping feature codes can explain this, challenging the general idea that an individual neuron necessarily has one interpretable job. It does not test any version's specified modern-model, InceptionV1, attribution-graph, or explanation-scoring conditions.
record.gate_note: The paper reports results about feature-channel codes and their use in small Boolean and toy-vision networks. Its explicit finding that a neuron responds to several AND features is relevant to the broad neuron-job premise, but does not test the listed version-specific audits or model classes. Other coding-pattern, scaling, and training results are not separate neuron-job measurements. Results cited from prior work were not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study works only on small trained MLPs: Boolean DNF and CNF tasks and a 128-input toy 'vision' task. It shows that neurons there are polysemantic through overlapping feature-channel codes, and that its weight-based method can read out the computation. None of this measures any version's construct. There are no neuron-job shares in language models (V1, V2) and no InceptionV1 neurons (V3). Nor is there a tool or architecture comparison of interpretable-neuron share (V4), an attribution graph on a large model (V5), or an explanation-versus-firing or simulation-scoring test (V7, V6). The record's 'tests/T5' contradicts its own finding that every version is not tested. The polysemanticity result is a related finding and belongs under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors propose that sign-based feature-channel codes in weights explain how small MLPs compute Boolean functions. Overlapping codes make neurons polysemantic, even when superposition is not needed. Packing limits on these codes explain error onset and a scaling law. Extension to deeper and production networks is preliminary or future work.
record.recipe_differences: The paper studies sign patterns and combinatorial feature-channel codes in small gradient-descent-trained Boolean and toy-vision MLPs. It does not use the neuron-explanation or activation-testing methods in the claim's original sources.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper notes that the input distribution affects the overall pattern frequencies, though not the described general scaling trends.

fits_no_version.finding: In small gradient-descent-trained Boolean MLPs, neurons take part in several overlapping feature-channel codes. For example, neuron 4 responds to 4 AND clauses. This polysemanticity appears even with more neurons than features (8 clauses, 16 neurons).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In small trained Boolean-task MLPs, overlapping combinatorial codes make neurons polysemantic even without capacity pressure.

fits_no_version.finding: A weight-only, code-based decoding of a toy 1D vision MLP recovers exact match positions 82.63% of the time. It is less accurate than the network itself on the binary decision (FPR 6.82% vs 0.71%; FNR 7.66% vs 1.65%).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Combinatorial weight analysis can partly recover feature computation in toy MLPs without trained replacement models.

record.problems: Evidence is limited to small, controlled Boolean and toy-vision networks; it does not establish prevalence in modern language models. The paper itself describes deeper-network disentanglement as preliminary and identifies real production-network computation as future work.
record.rows_left_out: No separate rows for the paper's numerous Boolean pattern-frequency and scaling plots: they measure feature-channel coding patterns and task error, not neuron-pole job shares or any other listed version.

untested.parts: No Qwen3-32B or any language-model neuron-pole audit.
No other language models, dense/MoE comparison or scale.
No InceptionV1 or canonical polysemantic neuron re-examination.
No comparison of interpretable-neuron share across tools, architectures or regularization.
No attribution graphs from a large model's neurons. Weight-based extraction is shown only in toy MLPs.
No test of activating-example explanations against where neurons fire.
No simulation-based automated scoring of neuron explanations.

record.verdict_notes: The relation was changed from tests/T5 to discusses/T6 because the record itself marks every version not tested and the paper uses no element of the claim. The study is a preprint with toy-scale evidence only. Any bearing on the claim is indirect: it argues that polysemanticity arises from combinatorial codes in tiny networks, which neither confirms nor refutes the essay's job-share figures for large models.

versions.untested_parts: No Qwen3-32B audit or neuron-pole job-share estimate.
No language-model comparison, dense/MoE comparison, or scaling to large or trillion-parameter models.
No InceptionV1 cat-and-car neuron or test of pose detection or recursive generalization.
No comparison of tools, architectures, regularization, or interpretability estimates for Inception-sized vision models.
No attribution-graph evaluation on a large model. The toy-vision code-extraction results are not that test.
No test of explanations against held-out activating examples or prediction of where neurons fire.
No automated neuron-explanation scoring on new text.

relation.reason: The paper discusses polysemanticity and superposition, with examples from its own toy networks. It tests no version.

tranche.reason: Toy Boolean MLPs (and a toy 1-D vision task) read with a static weight-sign method. No version's construct is measured: no LLM or vision-model neuron-pole job shares, no canonical-neuron reanalysis, no tool/architecture comparison of interpretable share, no attribution graphs, no explanation scoring.

source_check.notes: Both rows match the text, and the locators' section numbers (3.2, 3.4) are confirmed. The evidence is one representative toy network, so it gives no population estimate. In this paper 'polysemantic' neurons still sit inside computations the authors interpret fully from the weights. Its point that polysemanticity appears without capacity pressure only touches V4's 'not capacity' idea in passing and does not test it.

statements.correction: Neuron 4 of one representative run of a 2-layer MLP (16 inputs, 16 first-layer neurons) trained on an OR of 8 pairwise ANDs reacts positively to four AND clauses; Section 3.4 states polysemanticity appears even with fewer features (8 clauses) than neurons (16). Authors call the run typical of all such formulas.
